_comment: This list is short now, and its shortness is the point. Under the plugin distribution model the plugin itself carries the agents, skills, prompts, contexts, instructions, and the hook runtime, so none of them are copied into a consumer repository any more — the earlier fourteen-path subscription list existed only because there was no other delivery mechanism, and every path in it was a file that could drift, be edited locally, and then be silently overwritten by the next sync. Two things are still genuinely repo-local: the repo's own context file, which describes THIS codebase and is generated rather than synced (see repoContext below), and the install state at .github/orchestrator-install.json, which records what was actually written so uninstall and repair can be honest about it. The third entry, config/, is the one people are tempted to drop and should not: lib/config.js resolves configuration from <workspace>/.github/config/ first and falls back to the plugin's own defaults when it finds nothing, marking the result __fallback and continuing without an error. That fallback is correct behaviour for a hook that must not crash, and it is exactly why a missing config/ is dangerous — token budgets, stack mappings, redaction patterns, and the pipeline gates all quietly revert to built-in values and nothing in the session says a word about it.

subscriptions.why: The only content path that must reach the repository. Readers fall back to built-in defaults when it is absent and log nothing, so the failure mode is not a broken run but a run governed by values nobody chose.

vendoring.note: Vendoring copies plugin content into .github/ so it is readable offline and reviewable in the repo's own diff. It is opt-in, never the default, and connect-repo.ps1 only does it when passed -Vendor. The cost is the one the plugin model removed: a vendored repo needs a pull request per repository to take an upgrade, and every vendored file is a file someone can edit locally and then lose to the next sync. The ownership gate stays in place for that reason — a foreign file is skipped and reported rather than overwritten, and a file we wrote that has since changed is backed up before it is replaced.

repoContext.note: Generated by scripts/context-gen.py, not synced — it describes this repository, so there is no upstream copy of it to pull. Regenerating preserves the hand-written Integration Points and Verified Commands sections, because those hold knowledge no scan can recover. staleThresholdDays is the age at which the context is treated as suspect: fourteen days is short enough that a stale file is caught inside a normal sprint, and a stale context is worse than no context, since an agent reading a confidently wrong description of the codebase has no reason to go and look.
